objects.name: Pleiades
objects.notes: The blue reflection nebulosity around its brightest stars is an unrelated dust cloud the cluster is passing through; it is the separate Pleiades Nebula record. Gaia DR3 astrometry of Alcyone, Merope and Taygeta is too poor for Hunt & Reffert (2023) to list them; SIMBAD lists them as members. A Bayesian lithium-age model gives 124.5 (+3.3, −2.7) Myr (Chronos 2026 preprint, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25957). Space velocity from the mean Gaia DR3 proper motion and radial velocity of the members (Hunt & Reffert 2023).

objects.name: Trumpler 14
objects.notes: One of the youngest and densest clusters of the Carina Nebula, 0.2° from Eta Carinae and its cluster Trumpler 16. Its brightest star, HD 93129 A, is one of the hottest and most massive stars known. The mass of 890 ± 180 M☉ counts only the 96 members that Hunt & Reffert (2023) find in Gaia DR3; Portegies Zwart et al. (2010) list a photometric mass of about 10,000 M☉, among the young massive clusters. The distance is the Gaia EDR3 distance of its O and B stars (Villafranca O-002); Hunt & Reffert (2023) give 2,390 ± 11 pc from their members, statistical error only. Gaia DR3 measured the radial velocities of only seven members, hence the large error. No [Fe/H] is adopted. Space velocity from the mean Gaia DR3 proper motion and radial velocity of the members (Hunt & Reffert 2023).

objects.name: Omega Centauri
objects.notes: The most massive globular cluster of the Milky Way. Its stars formed over more than a billion years and differ widely in iron, so it is thought to be the core of a dwarf galaxy the Milky Way swallowed. [Fe/H] is the Harris (1996) value on the Carretta et al. (2009) scale, a mean over its populations. Space velocity from the Gaia EDR3 proper motion (Vasiliev & Baumgardt 2021) and the mean radial velocity of the members.

objects.name: Terzan 5
objects.notes: Hidden behind thick dust near the Galactic center and seen mostly in infrared light. It holds the most millisecond pulsars of any cluster. Long classed as a globular cluster, it formed stars in several bursts and is now thought to be a fossil fragment of the young Galactic bulge. [Fe/H] and the age are those of the dominant old population; the main younger population, 4.7 ± 0.5 billion years old (Zullo et al. 2026), is richer in iron than the Sun, [Fe/H] = +0.27 (Origlia et al. 2011). The Carretta et al. (2009) value, +0.16 from the Harris (1996) catalog, blends both and is not adopted; Ferraro et al. (2016) gave 12 ± 1 billion years for the old population. Space velocity from the Gaia EDR3 proper motion (Vasiliev & Baumgardt 2021) and the mean radial velocity of the members.

objects.name: Westerlund 1
objects.notes: The most massive young cluster known in the Milky Way, hidden behind thick dust. It holds 24 Wolf–Rayet stars, yellow hypergiants, red supergiants such as Westerlund 1 W26, and the magnetar CXOU J164710.2−455216. Its velocity dispersion gives a dynamical mass of about 63,000 M☉ (log M = 4.8, Portegies Zwart et al. 2010). Its age is debated: Beasor et al. (2021) find 10.4 (+1.3/−1.2) million years from its red supergiants, much older than the 3.5–5 million years of earlier work. The TeV gamma-ray source HESS J1646−458 surrounds it. Age, mass and radii: Portegies Zwart et al. (2010), unless the age names its own source. No space motion is adopted.

objects.name: Arches Cluster

Dust hides it in visible light, so it is studied in infrared light, radio waves and X-rays. It holds 13 Wolf–Rayet stars and eight O hypergiants; its X-rays suggest that many of its massive stars are close binaries. Age, mass and radii: Portegies Zwart et al. objects.name: Quintuplet Cluster

It holds the Pistol Star, a candidate luminous blue variable, placed at the same distance. Like the Arches Cluster, it is hidden in visible light and studied in infrared light, radio waves and X-rays. Its hot stars ionize the Sickle Nebula. Age, mass and radii: Portegies Zwart et al. objects.notes: The central concentration of the cluster NGC 2070, at the heart of the Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud. It holds the most massive stars known, among them R136a1, and produces most of the light that makes the nebula glow. Portegies Zwart et al. (2010) list 3 million years from earlier work. The distance is that of the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Tarantula Nebula record. Age, mass and radii: Portegies Zwart et al. (2010), unless the age names its own source. objects.name: RSGC1
objects.notes: A cluster of 14 red supergiants at the base of the Scutum–Centaurus arm, near the end of the Galactic bar, hidden behind thick dust and found in 2006 in 2MASS images. With Stephenson 2 and RSGC3 nearby, it belongs to a burst of star formation 10–20 million years ago. Davies et al. (2008) estimate an initial mass of (3 ± 1) × 10^4 M☉.
